key_terms.meaning: A model that gives a sentence probability P(w1...wT)=∏P(wt | previous n−1 words) for order n.
The probability of the next word depends only on the previous n−1 words, not the whole history.
For an n-gram, P(wt | context)=count(context, wt) ÷ count(context), read directly from a corpus.
Moving a small amount of probability mass from seen n-grams to unseen n-grams so no event gets zero.
P(wt | context)=(count(context, wt)+1) ÷ (count(context)+V), where V is vocabulary size.
A weighted mix of models of different orders, such as λP(trigram)+(1−λ)P(bigram).
Use a lower-order model when the higher-order n-gram count is zero.
PP=P(w1...wT)^(−1/T), the inverse geometric mean probability per test word; lower is better.
A test token not present in the model vocabulary; it cannot receive a normal n-gram probability.
The grammatical class of a token, such as noun, verb, adjective or postposition.
The fixed set of part-of-speech labels used by a tagger, for example Penn Treebank tags.
Tag every word with the tag it had most often in training data; a simple but strong baseline.
A model with hidden tag states and observed words, using transition and emission probabilities.
Dynamic programming over a trellis that finds the single most probable hidden tag path.
A sequence model that scores each tag with a log-linear classifier over previous tag and many features, normalised per position.
A sequence model that scores the whole label sequence with one log-linear function and normalises once over all sequences.
Finding text spans that name people, places, organisations, dates and similar categories.
A span encoding where B-X starts an entity of type X, I-X continues it, and O is outside any entity.
Finding a relation between two named entities and outputting a subject, relation, object triple.
A structured fact in the form (subject, relation, object), such as (Chennai, located_in, Tamil Nadu).

takeaways: An n-gram language model turns a sentence probability into a product of local conditional probabilities estimated by counts.
Unseen n-grams get zero without smoothing, so smoothing is essential for any real test text.
Interpolation and backoff combine models of different orders to handle sparse counts.
Perplexity is lower and better when the model gives higher probability to the test words.
Part-of-speech tagging assigns a grammatical class to every token and can draw knowledge from rules, annotated data or learned transformations.
A hidden Markov model treats tags as hidden states and words as observations, and Viterbi finds the best tag path.
A maximum entropy Markov model uses many overlapping features but normalises at each position.
A conditional random field normalises over whole label sequences and avoids scoring each position in isolation.
Named entity recognition is usually sequence labelling, and BIO tags encode entity spans.
Information extraction fills structured slots, and relation extraction links two entities into a triple.
bank_note: Long answers usually ask for definitions with formulas, a small worked count or trellis, and a comparison of sequence models on features, normalisation and label bias.

bank.q: Explain an n-gram language model. Write the chain-rule form, state the Markov assumption, and give the maximum likelihood estimate for an n-gram.
Why do unsmoothed n-gram models assign zero probability to unseen n-grams? Explain add-one smoothing, interpolation and backoff.
outline: Add-one formula and vocabulary size V

bank.q: Define perplexity of a language model. Derive it from the probability of a test sentence and explain why lower perplexity is better.
outline: Lower PP means higher average word probability
Compare only on same tokenisation and vocabulary

bank.q: Compare rule-based, stochastic and transformation-based part-of-speech tagging. Where does each tagger get its knowledge from?
Describe a hidden Markov model for part-of-speech tagging. Define transition and emission probabilities and explain how Viterbi finds the best tag sequence.
outline: Hidden states are tags; observations are words

bank.q: Explain maximum entropy Markov models and conditional random fields. How do they differ in features and in normalisation?
outline: CRF normalises once over all sequences

bank.q: Explain named entity recognition and relation extraction. How does BIO tagging encode a named entity span, and what is a relation triple?
outline: Relation extraction as linking two entities

bank.q: A tiny corpus has the bigram 'cup tea' twice, 'cup coffee' once, and vocabulary size V=3 for the context 'cup'. Compute P(tea | cup) and P(coffee | cup) with maximum likelihood and with add-one smoothing.
Given start, transition and emission probabilities for a two-tag HMM, show the first two columns of the Viterbi trellis for a short word sequence.
outline: Recurrence uses max over previous tags

bank.q: Design features for a MEMM or CRF part-of-speech tagger. Include word, context, suffix and unknown-word features, and state where normalisation happens.
outline: MEMM normalises per position; CRF normalises globally

bank.q: Build a simple named entity recognition pipeline using tokenisation, BIO tags and a sequence labeller. State the training and evaluation steps.
outline: Features such as word, shape and context
Evaluate span-level precision, recall and F1

bank.q: Compare HMM, MEMM and CRF for sequence labelling. Discuss features, normalisation, label bias and training cost.
outline: Rich overlapping features in MEMM and CRF

bank.q: A language model reports lower perplexity after a change in tokenisation. Is it necessarily a better model? Discuss vocabulary, OOV rate and comparability.
outline: Intrinsic score is not the same as task quality

bank.q: You must tag a new domain with no labelled data. Compare rule-based, stochastic and transformation-based tagging on annotation cost, domain shift, unknown words and ambiguity.
outline: Transformation-based needs seed tagger and data

glossary.def: A collection of text used for training or evaluating a language model or tagger.
A word, punctuation mark or other small unit produced by tokenisation.
The process of splitting raw text into tokens.
The set of distinct tokens known to a model.
A sequence of n consecutive tokens, such as a bigram or trigram.
A probability estimate obtained by dividing an event count by the relevant context count.
A method that gives some probability to unseen events.
Smoothing that adds one to every count and adjusts the denominator by vocabulary size.
A weighted combination of probability estimates from models of different orders.
A method that falls back to a shorter context when a longer context has zero count.
A measure of how well a language model predicts a test text; lower is better.
A token in test data that is absent from the model vocabulary.
A grammatical category such as noun, verb, adjective or postposition.
The complete list of part-of-speech labels used in a tagging task.
A part-of-speech class that readily accepts new words, such as nouns and verbs.
A part-of-speech class with a small fixed membership, such as pronouns and prepositions.
The case where one word form can receive more than one part-of-speech tag.
A probabilistic model with hidden states and observed outputs, used here for tagging.
The probability of moving from one hidden tag to the next.
The probability of observing a word given a hidden tag.
A dynamic programming algorithm that finds the highest-probability hidden state path.
A sequence model that uses a log-linear classifier at each position and normalises locally.
A sequence model that scores whole label sequences and normalises globally.
The task of finding and classifying names and similar entity spans in text.
A tag scheme where B starts an entity, I continues it and O marks outside text.
The task of identifying a relation between two entities and forming a triple.
